labels.why: Salesforce enforces execution limits, and the bot must keep each transaction within the limits that apply to its callouts and processing.
The bot can answer with a synchronous callout, so it can work without enqueuing a job.
Each Grok call has a finite context window, which bounds how much of the question and conversation history can be sent together.
The model's input and output token limits bound the questions the bot can accept in one call and the answers it can return from it.
The bot can report a result or a callout failure when it occurs without promising an end-to-end answer time.
The app can keep adding people in order even when all class seats are taken, without setting a maximum waitlist length.
The app can offer an open seat right up to class start without requiring any minimum lead time.
The app can give the next eligible person the available seat without guaranteeing promotion within a fixed time after cancellation.
Automation needs a rule for when an unpaid invoice triggers its first reminder and any repeats, even if reminders continue until payment.
The sending service has finite throughput, so a large batch must adapt to the rate the service accepts.
A reminder can go out whenever it becomes due, including outside local business hours or on a holiday.
The app can send all pending reminders as capacity permits, checking that each invoice is still unpaid, without a volume cap or lateness deadline.
The upload path has finite capacity, so the importer must handle files beyond what that path can accept, even if it streams rows.
Bulk creation can provision accounts without sending invitation or welcome mail, so it need not impose a mail pacing rule.
An accepted import can finish as processing capacity becomes available without guaranteeing a maximum completion time.
